definition: In classical logic, propositions are typically unambiguously considered as being true or false.
details: For instance, the proposition one is both equal and not equal to itself is regarded as simply false, being contrary to the Law of Noncontradiction; while the proposition one is equal to one is regarded as simply true, by the Law of Identity. However, some mathematicians, computer scientists, and philosophers have been attracted to the idea that a proposition might be more or less true, rather than wholly true or wholly false. Consider this pizza is hot. In mathematics, this idea can be developed in terms of fuzzy logic. In computer science, it has found application in artificial intelligence. In philosophy, the idea has proved particularly appealing in the case of vagueness. Degrees of truth is an important concept in law. The term is an older concept than conditional probability. Instead of determining the objective probability, only a subjective assessment is defined. In adjudicative processes, 'substantive truth' is distinct from 'formal legal truth' which comes in four degrees: hearsay, balance of probabilities, proven beyond reasonable doubt and absolute truth (knowledge reserved unto God).

explainer.lead: Degree of truth is the idea that a statement can be more or less true, instead of simply true or false. It offers a way to handle vague descriptions such as “this pizza is hot,” and also appears in artificial intelligence, philosophy, and law.

tiers.eli5: Imagine saying whether a pizza is hot. A slice just out of the oven fits “hot” very well, a lukewarm slice fits it a little, and a cold slice barely fits it at all. Degree of truth lets us describe those shades instead of forcing every answer into yes or no.
tiers.practitioner: In computer science, degrees of truth can be developed through fuzzy logic and applied in artificial intelligence. They are useful for vague statements that do not have a clean true-or-false boundary. A key pitfall is treating a subjective assessment of truth as though it were an objective probability.
tiers.paperLevel: Classical logic assigns a proposition P a binary status, true or false; degree-of-truth approaches instead represent P as being more or less true. Fuzzy logic provides a mathematical development of this idea. The notion differs from conditional probability: it defines a subjective assessment rather than determining an objective probability.

explainer.example: For “this pizza is hot,” a freshly baked pizza supports the statement strongly, a lukewarm pizza supports it only partly, and a cold pizza supports it very weakly. Instead of drawing one arbitrary line between hot and not hot, the three cases receive different degrees of truth.

usedIn.name: Artificial intelligence
usedIn.detail: Applies the computer-science development of propositions that can be more or less true.

usedIn.name: Fuzzy logic
usedIn.detail: Provides a mathematical framework for degrees of truth.

usedIn.name: Philosophy
usedIn.detail: Helps address vagueness, where a sharp true-or-false boundary is unappealing.

usedIn.name: Law
usedIn.detail: Distinguishes substantive truth from formal legal truth and its degrees.

explainer.intuition: Some statements fit a situation completely, some partly, and some hardly at all. Degree of truth captures that variation rather than forcing every proposition into one of two categories.
howItWorks: Start with a proposition, such as “this pizza is hot.”
Ask how well the proposition fits, rather than only whether it is true or false.
Treat stronger fits as more true and weaker fits as less true.
Use fuzzy logic when a mathematical treatment is needed, while keeping the assessment distinct from objective probability.
explainer.whyItMatters: The idea provides a way to reason about vagueness and supports applications in artificial intelligence. In law, it also helps frame distinctions among hearsay, balance of probabilities, proof beyond reasonable doubt, and absolute truth.
misconceptions: A degree of truth is not an objective probability; it is a subjective assessment rather than a calculation of conditional probability.
Accepting degrees of truth does not mean classical true-or-false reasoning disappears: “one is equal to one” remains simply true under the Law of Identity.
